clues.title: Plate: long white, blue left, yellow right
text: Portuguese plates are long and white, with a blue strip on the left. Most plates have a **yellow strip** on the right, which is unique to Portugal.
The yellow strip was discontinued in 2020, so in Generation 4 coverage you may sometimes see plates with just the blue strip.
clues.summary: Long white plates with a blue strip on the left and, on most, a yellow strip on the right, which is unique. The yellow strip stopped in 2020, so Gen 4 may show plates with only the blue strip.

clues.title: Language: Ç Ã Õ Â Ê, no Ñ
text: **Portuguese** is a Romance language that is closely related to Spanish. Unlike Spanish, Portuguese includes the letters Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, and Ê, while it does not include the letter Ñ, which is very common in Spanish.
NOTE: You can also find Ç in Catalan.

images.caption: Portuguese text with Ç Ã Õ Â Ê shown large

clues.summary: A Romance language close to Spanish, with the letters Ç, Ã, Õ, Â and Ê but no Ñ. Ç is also used in Catalan.

differs.how: Spanish has Ñ and lacks Ã and Õ

clues.title: Plants: eucalyptus trees
text: **Eucalyptus trees** are very common in Portugal. The only other part of Europe where you’ll commonly see eucalyptus is [northern Spain](https://www.google.com/maps/@43.1615813,-8.7773429,3a,90y,44.89h,89.75t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sC7quFqkQ-yqtdhYH-ACW8w!2e0!7i13312!8i6656?entry=ttu).
clues.summary: Eucalyptus is very common. The only other part of Europe where it is common is northern Spain.

clues.title: Language: street is 'Rua'
text: The Portuguese word for road is **‘Rua’**.
NOTE: In Galician, the word for road is ‘Rúa’, with an accent on the ‘u’.
clues.summary: The word for road is Rua. In Galicia, in northern Spain, it is spelled Rúa with an accent.

differs.how: Galicia writes Rúa with an accent

clues.title: Pole: concrete ladder pole, tall steps
text: Concrete ladder poles, with very **tall ladder steps**, are common in Portugal. Each step often has a small [see-through hole](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vDoNQJNkY2srorxc8).

NOTE: In [Spain](https://www.google.com/maps/@43.5609502,-8.1852362,3a,32.9y,335.94h,91.24t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sRl489cMP23rutAjdJsp5KA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) and [France](https://goo.gl/maps/cYtpBcr8fPxdawT1A) you will commonly see ladder poles with short steps.
clues.summary: Concrete ladder poles with very tall steps, often with a small see-through hole in each step. Spain and France have ladder poles with short steps.

differs.how: Spanish ladder poles have short steps
French ladder poles have short steps

clues.title: Sign: hunting sign, red and white
text: **Hunting signs** with a red and white colour scheme are a common sight in rural areas. They are either diamond shaped or rectangular.

NOTE: In contrast, [Spanish](https://www.google.com/maps/@39.9083771,-2.5360346,3a,15y,154.88h,76.9t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1se3LYRFex8eXCgocKMCvxPw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) hunting signs are white and black.
clues.summary: Red-and-white hunting signs, diamond or rectangular, are common in the countryside. Spanish hunting signs are white and black.

differs.how: Spanish hunting signs are white and black

clues.title: Bollard: thin white wedge or flat, wide reflector
text: Portuguese bollards are either wedge-shaped with a noticeably thin white top, or flat with a wide reflector. While most reflectors will be white, you may also find [orange](https://goo.gl/maps/5tWaAjwR2XWPHigU8) reflectors. These are noticeably darker than the [yellow reflectors](https://www.google.com/maps/@41.9861981,-5.1213523,3a,19.2y,201.17h,74.37t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sJ3baT-DirwydAJfMwHD0Pg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) in Spain.
clues.summary: Either a wedge with a noticeably thin white top, or a flat post with a wide reflector. Reflectors are mostly white, sometimes orange, which is darker than Spain's yellow.

clues.title: Direction sign: white, black arrows off the edge
text: Directional signs are generally white, with **black arrows** that are **not** touching the borders of the sign.
NOTE: [Spanish](https://goo.gl/maps/NdKZE9FwK2q66enj6) directional signs will typically feature the road number in colourful boxes and do not have a black arrow, other than a thin black border.
clues.summary: White signs with black arrows that do not touch the sign's border. Spanish signs show road numbers in coloured boxes and have no black arrow, only a thin black border.

differs.how: Spanish signs use coloured road-number boxes, no black arrow

clues.title: Route marker: coloured diagonal block on left
text: Most kilometre markers are wide rectangles with a **coloured section** on the left side divided diagonally from the white part. Every kilometre you will find a larger [square sign](https://goo.gl/maps/d31pnwB3RjC8JZWD8) with a coloured top half featuring the road number.
clues.summary: Most kilometre markers are wide rectangles with a coloured section on the left, split diagonally from the white part. Every kilometre there is a bigger square sign with a coloured top half showing the road number.

clues.title: Waystone: black and white
text: Black and white waystones can commonly be found in Portugal.
clues.summary: Black and white waystones are common.

clues.title: Sign: stop with big font
text: Stop signs in Portugal feature a fairly large font.

NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish it from [Spain](https://www.google.com/maps/@41.4989864,-1.390895,3a,15y,67.65h,81.9t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sPtHx268nIZR2fqVugwTlsQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu), where stop signs have a distinctly small and compact font.
clues.summary: Stop signs use a fairly large font. Spanish stop signs have a small, compact font.

differs.how: Spanish stop lettering is small and compact

clues.title: Chevron: black with yellow arrows
text: Portuguese chevrons are **black with yellow arrows**.
NOTE: Portugal is the only Mediterranean country with this chevron colour scheme.
clues.summary: Black chevrons with yellow arrows. The only Mediterranean country with this colour scheme.

clues.title: Pedestrian sign: five stripes, high belt
text: Pedestrian signs have **five stripes**, and the person is wearing a **belt**, which is noticeably high.

NOTE: [Spanish pedestrian signs](https://goo.gl/maps/tsQ3wkTxKwZuebwp9) have eight stripes, [Italian signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/RiDqBuojwMhYqgDCA) don't have a belt and [Greek signs](https://goo.gl/maps/RCxiJ5SWmjfFM3TB8) have two dotted lines instead of stripes.
clues.summary: Five stripes and a person wearing a noticeably high belt. Spanish signs have eight stripes, Italian figures have no belt, and Greek signs have two dotted lines instead of stripes.

differs.how: Greek signs have two dotted lines

clues.title: Guardrail: A-type with red reflectors
text: Portugal uses A-type guardrails with **red reflectors**.
NOTE: This is mostly useful to tell apart Portugal and [Spain](https://goo.gl/maps/shMgzeFPhLmZMiqX6), which uses yellow reflectors.
clues.summary: A-type guardrails with red reflectors. Spain's have yellow reflectors.

clues.title: Sign: road signs with white border
text: Portuguese road signs are typically encased by a **white border**.
NOTE: Most [Spanish](https://www.google.com/maps/@38.8639722,-4.7943486,3a,17.5y,29.06h,88.7t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1swJ7te-wPHR9taiHRqU2LIg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) signs don’t have a white border.
clues.summary: Road signs usually have a white border around them. Most Spanish signs do not.

differs.how: Most Spanish signs have no white border

clues.title: Road: cobblestones set diagonally
text: Cobblestone roads are very common in Portugal. These will typically be made of square cobblestones arranged **diagonally** compared to the road direction.
clues.summary: Cobblestone roads are very common, usually square stones laid diagonally to the road direction.

clues.title: Sidewalk: bright cobblestones
text: Similarly, cobblestone sidewalks made of distinctly **bright stones** are very common.
clues.summary: Cobblestone sidewalks made of distinctly bright stones are very common.

clues.title: Houses: white stone, orange tiled roof
text: White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common in Portugal.
clues.summary: White-painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common.

clues.title: Houses: blue or yellow paint lines
text: You’ll commonly see **blue or yellow lines** painted around windows and doors, as well as around the edges of walls.
clues.summary: Blue or yellow lines are painted around windows, doors and wall edges.

clues.title: Houses: decorative mosaic tiles
text: Houses made of **decorative mosaic tiles** are somewhat common in Portugal.

images.caption: Circle at top left magnifies the blue and white decorative tile pattern covering the house facade

clues.summary: Houses covered in decorative mosaic tiles are fairly common.

clues.title: Google car: low camera, big round blur
text: Portugal has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

clues.summary: A Gen 4 camera mounted lower than usual, with a big round blur and a small bump at the front. The blur can be see-through, which makes it easy to miss.

clues.title: Phone numbers: first three digits show the region
text: The first three digits of Portuguese landlines make up the **area codes**, which are distributed as seen on the map. Phone codes not starting with a 2 are not regional, and codes starting with 29 will either be the Azores or Madeira.
For a complete list of the third digits, see [this page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone_numbers_in_Portugal#Prefix_list).
clues.summary: The first three digits of a landline are the area code, and they are spread out by region. Codes not starting with 2 are not regional, and codes starting with 29 are Azores or Madeira.

clues.title: Houses: decorative chimneys, round or square
text: In the Faro district in the south of Portugal you will very commonly come across decorative chimneys, which will either be round or square shaped with small spire-shaped tops. The round chimneys are a particularly strong clue.
clues.summary: In the southern Faro district, decorative chimneys are very common, round or square with small spire tops. The round ones are a strong clue.

clues.title: Houses: square concrete blocks, white mortar
text: Houses in northern Portugal are often made of **square concrete blocks**, which are commonly put together with white mortar.
NOTE: Very similar architecture, but typically without the white mortar, is commonly found over the border in [Galicia](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kp1QuJLF1w3t65b59).
clues.summary: In the north, houses are often made of square concrete blocks joined with white mortar. Over the border in Galicia it looks similar, usually without white mortar.

differs.how: Spanish Galicia usually has no white mortar

clues.title: Landscape: open fields with holm and cork oaks
text: Open fields sparsely populated with **holm oaks** ([Quercus ilex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_ilex)) and **cork oaks** ([Quercus suber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_suber)) are very common in the southeast. These species of oaks tend to be on the smaller side, and have a Mediterranean look. While these fields will look quite dry during summer and fall, they will look [much lusher](https://maps.app.goo.gl/N1VwqNrQLgsqpAnm8) during spring.
clues.summary: In the southeast, open fields sparsely dotted with small Mediterranean-looking holm and cork oaks. They look dry in summer and autumn and much lusher in spring.

clues.title: Plants: olive plantations in dense rows
text: **Olive plantations** are generally more common in the eastern half of the country, particularly in the far northeast and slight southeast.

NOTE: The easiest way to tell apart the olive plantations from the oak fields from the last tip is to look at the pattern in which they’re planted. Olive plantations are typically planted in dense rows, while the oaks are planted more sparsely and not in an obvious pattern.
clues.summary: Olive plantations are more common in the eastern half, especially the far northeast and a bit of the southeast. Olives are planted in dense rows; the oaks of the previous tip are sparse with no pattern.

clues.title: Plants: dense eucalyptus forests
text: Dense **eucalyptus forests** are mostly found in the northwest.
clues.summary: Dense eucalyptus forests are mostly in the northwest.

clues.title: Plants: maritime pine, grey-red bark, fluffy tops
text: Forests, or plantations of** Maritime pines **([Pinus Pinaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_pinaster)) are very common in the northern half of Portugal. You can recognize the tree by its grey bark with red undertones, and fluffy branches that point upwards. Older trees often don’t have any branches in the bottom half of the tree.
NOTE: Plantations of this pine are also common in northern Spain, particularly Galicia.
clues.summary: Forests or plantations of maritime pine are very common in the northern half. Grey bark with red undertones, fluffy upward branches, and old trees often bare in the lower half. Also common in northern Spain.

clues.title: Landscape: steep terraced vineyards
text: In the [Douro wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douro_DOC), straight east of Porto, you will commonly find **steep terraced vineyards**.
clues.summary: In the Douro wine region, east of Porto, steep terraced vineyards are common.

clues.title: Plants: citrus plantations
text: **Citrus plantations** are mostly found along the south coast.
clues.summary: Citrus plantations are mostly along the south coast.

clues.title: Coverage: islands count as the mainland country
text: The islands of Madeira and the Azores are found southwest and west of mainland Portugal respectively. For country streak purposes they are both counted as Portugal.
Plonk It has more in-depth guides to Madeira [here](https://www.plonkit.net/madeira) and a guide to the Azores [here](https://www.plonkit.net/azores).
clues.summary: Madeira (southwest) and the Azores (west) both count as the same country for streak purposes.

clues.title: Landscape: rocky highland, striped snow poles
text: The Serra da Estrela natural park can be recognised by the **rocky mountainous highland landscape**, often combined with yellow and black striped snow poles.

images.caption: Mountain road; the red circle zooms in on a striped snow pole, left

clues.summary: A rocky mountainous highland, often with yellow-and-black striped snow poles (Serra da Estrela park).

clues.title: Landscape: pine forest on very white sandy soil
text: Pine forests with extremely **sandy white soil** can be found near the coast between the cities of Setúbal and Sines.
clues.summary: Near the coast between Setúbal and Sines, pine forests grow on extremely sandy white soil.

clues.title: Landscape: flat, dry, almost treeless
text: In the far southwest of the country you can find a flat uncultivated landscape with very limited vegetation, which typically appears quite dry. There are almost no trees nearby, and only very low bushes and grass.
clues.summary: In the far southwest, flat uncultivated land that looks dry, with almost no trees and only low bushes and grass.

clues.title: Street sign: lime green
text: **Lime green street signs** can be found in Porto.
clues.summary: Lime green street signs are found in Porto.

clues.title: Pole: mainland-style infrastructure on islands
text: Since the Azores is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles, chevrons and bollards.
clues.summary: The Azores are an autonomous region, so poles, chevrons and bollards look like those on the mainland.

clues.title: Landscape: rolling fields, round hills behind
text: Most of the Azores visible on Street View consists of open agricultural fields in a rolling landscape, often with taller round hills in the background.
NOTE: Madeira has a very mountainous landscape, and very rarely has open agricultural fields.
clues.summary: Most Azores coverage shows open farm fields in rolling land, often with taller round hills behind. Madeira is very mountainous and rarely has open fields.

clues.title: Wall: dry rock walls of volcanic stone
text: **Dry rock walls** made of volcanic rocks are very common on the Azores.
NOTE: Dry rock walls are not common on Madeira, and while they are somewhat common on mainland Portugal, they will not be made of volcanic rocks.
clues.summary: Dry walls of volcanic rock are very common on the Azores. They are rare on Madeira, and mainland ones are not volcanic.

clues.title: Plants: hydrangeas
text: **Hydrangeas** can commonly be seen on the Azores.
NOTE: They can rarely be found on Madeira.
clues.summary: Hydrangeas are common on the Azores and rarely seen on Madeira.

clues.title: Plants: Japanese cedar
text: Japanese cedars ([cryptomeria japonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptomeria)) are very common on the Azores.
NOTE: While they can less commonly be seen on Madeira, they are not native to any part of mainland Europe.
clues.summary: Japanese cedars are very common on the Azores. They are less common on Madeira and not native to mainland Europe.

clues.title: Houses: low, white or pastel, grey trim
text: Houses in the Azores are typically one or two stories, with an orange tiled roof. They are painted **white** or in **pastel colours**, and dark green shutters on windows are common.

While you can also find [yellow](https://maps.app.goo.gl/eKrCqxAGLvi8JfKr8) or [blue](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tztY4hFYy1q7exjYA) highlights like in mainland Portugal, **grey highlights** are almost exclusive to the Azores.
clues.summary: Houses are one or two storeys with orange tiled roofs, painted white or pastel, often with dark green shutters. Yellow or blue trim is like the mainland, but grey trim is almost only on the Azores.

clues.title: Street sign: painted ceramic tile, blue letters
text: Street signs in the Azores are almost exclusively painted ceramic tiles, with blue letters and, typically, a decorative pattern around the edge.
clues.summary: Street signs are almost always painted ceramic tiles with blue letters and usually a decorative edge.

clues.title: Direction sign: striped signpost
text: Signposts on the Azores are often striped.
NOTE: These are also seen on Madeira.
clues.summary: Signposts are often striped, as on Madeira.

clues.title: Animals: black and white cows
text: **Black and white cows** are very common on the Azores.
NOTE: Cows on Madeira are usually [brown with white spots](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6cXY7T6okctmsJ9FA).
clues.summary: Black and white cows are very common on the Azores. On Madeira cows are usually brown with white spots.

clues.title: Coverage: car coverage on only three islands
text: The only islands in the Azores with car coverage are Ilha de São Miguel, Ilha Terceira and Ilha do Faial.
clues.summary: Only São Miguel, Terceira and Faial have car coverage.

clues.title: Coverage: Gen 4 on only one island
text: The only island with **Generation 4** coverage is Ilha de São Miguel.
clues.summary: Only São Miguel has Gen 4 coverage.

clues.title: Coverage: low-quality camera, dented or smooth car
text: **Shitcam** coverage is found on Ilha de São Miguel and Ilha do Faial.

The car seen on [São Miguel](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JAvRHWSUTF1WN64C8) has an **indentation** in the centre, while the one on [Faial](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SFnsE3SAKAeeX8Pw7) appears as a smooth surface, sometimes with an antenna visible.
clues.summary: The low-quality camera is on São Miguel and Faial. On São Miguel the car has a dent in the middle; on Faial it looks smooth, sometimes with an antenna.

clues.title: Landscape: lakes on an island
text: Ilha de São Miguel is the only island in the Azores or Madeira where you can find lakes.
clues.summary: São Miguel is the only island in the Azores or Madeira with lakes.

clues.title: Wall: rock wall with white painted concrete top
text: Rock walls with a white painted concrete top are somewhat common on Ilha Terceira.
clues.summary: Rock walls topped with white-painted concrete are fairly common on Terceira.

clues.title: Wall: whitewashed with dark basalt stones
text: On Ilha do Faial, you will sometimes find traditional whitewashed rock walls with unevenly sized dark basalt stones.

images.caption: Circle zooms in on the black volcanic stones set in the whitewashed wall

clues.summary: On Faial you sometimes see traditional whitewashed rock walls with unevenly sized dark basalt stones.

clues.title: Coverage: walking trekker along a crater rim
text: A trekker going along the edge of a crater can be seen on Ilha do Faial.
clues.summary: A trekker walking along a crater edge on Faial.

clues.title: Pole: mainland-style infrastructure on island
text: Since Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles and chevrons.
clues.summary: Madeira is an autonomous region, so poles and chevrons look like those on the mainland.

clues.title: Landscape: very mountainous, semi-tropical island
text: Madeira is a very mountainous and semi-tropical island.
NOTE: The Azores are less mountainous and more temperate.
clues.summary: Madeira is very mountainous and semi-tropical. The Azores are less mountainous and cooler.

clues.title: Plants: eucalyptus forests
text: Similar to continental Portugal, Madeira has a lot of **eucalyptus forests**, which can sometimes look deceptively [like the mainland](https://maps.app.goo.gl/iPZqubcw1HMTrzAi9).
NOTE: The Azores do not commonly have eucalypti.
clues.summary: Madeira has lots of eucalyptus forest that can look like the mainland. The Azores rarely have eucalyptus.

clues.title: Plants: occasional hydrangeas
text: **Hydrangeas** can occasionally be seen.
NOTE: They are even more common on the Azores.
clues.summary: Hydrangeas appear occasionally on Madeira but are more common on the Azores.

clues.title: Plants: African lily, blue or white flowers
text: African lilies ([Agapanthus praecox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agapanthus_praecox)) are very common in Madeira. They can be recognized by their long grassy leaves and round flower clusters at the end of a long stem. The most common colours are white and [blue](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tjbb37GMwtSgrUNb6).
clues.summary: African lilies are very common: long grassy leaves and round flower clusters on a tall stem, most often white or blue.

clues.title: Landscape: terraced farms with stone walls
text: Due to the lack of flat terrain, **terrace farming** is extensively practised on the island. Stone walls are used to separate the individual plateaus.
clues.summary: With so little flat land, terrace farming is widespread, with stone walls between the plateaus.

clues.title: Plants: ferns everywhere
text: **Ferns** are very common throughout the island.
clues.summary: Ferns are very common across the island.

clues.title: Houses: white, grey or pastel, tidy red roofs
text: Houses are mainly painted white, grey, or pastel colours such as yellow and pink. In addition, the red tile roofs will often be in a good condition.
clues.summary: Houses are mainly white, grey or pastel yellow and pink, and the red tile roofs are often in good condition.

clues.title: Guardrail: concrete block barriers
text: **Concrete block barriers**, usually painted white, are often found along roads.
clues.summary: Concrete block barriers, usually painted white, often line the roads.

clues.title: Sign: bus stop in black, white and yellow
text: Bus stops signs on Madeira follow a unique **black, white **and** yellow** colour scheme.
clues.summary: Bus stop signs use a unique black, white and yellow colour scheme.

clues.title: Taxi: yellow with blue stripe
text: Taxis on Madeira are yellow with a blue stripe running along the sides of the car.
clues.summary: Taxis are yellow with a blue stripe along the sides.

clues.title: Bollard: small stone, red reflector
text: Madeira commonly uses small and unique stone bollards with a red reflector. They are either cuboidal or cylindrical in shape.
clues.summary: Small, unique stone bollards with a red reflector, either box-shaped or round.

clues.title: Guardrail: yellow and black
text: Madeira sometimes uses yellow-and black guardrails on its mountain roads.
clues.summary: Yellow-and-black guardrails sometimes appear on mountain roads.

clues.title: Sign: unique speed limit signs on highways
text: These speed limit signs are unique to Madeira and can be found on its highways.
clues.summary: Special speed limit signs unique to Madeira on its highways.

clues.title: Landscape: low clouds
text: **Low altitude **clouds are typical on the island, and are often seen on street view.
clues.summary: Low clouds are typical on the island and often show up in Street View.

clues.title: Coverage: foggy
text: **Foggy coverage** is quite common.
clues.summary: Foggy coverage is quite common.

clues.title: Landscape: many tunnels
text: As a result of the island’s mountainous terrain, **tunnels** are very common.
clues.summary: Because of the mountains, tunnels are very common.

clues.title: Bridge: dark green railings
text: On bridges you will often find railings painted **dark green**.
clues.summary: Bridges often have dark green railings.

clues.title: Direction sign: striped signpost
text: Signposts on Madeira are often striped.
NOTE: These are also seen on the Azores.
clues.summary: Signposts are often striped, as on the Azores.

clues.title: Sign: loose cows warning, brown with white
text: You can sometimes find **free roaming cows** on high-altitude roads on the island, as well as warning signs for those cows. The cows will typically be brown with white spots, contrary to the Azores, where the cows will typically be [black and white](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vsM6TJ2DnHi1vKEG7).
clues.summary: On high roads you can find free-roaming cows and warning signs for them. They are usually brown with white spots, unlike the black and white cows of the Azores.

clues.title: Coverage: gloomy low-quality camera, white car
text: Google used a weird, low-quality camera on Madeira, commonly known as the official Ari (or "shitcam"). It has a wide circular car blur and makes the image appear rather gloomy. On Madeira, you will often see the unblurred back of a **white** car.
A good map will usually not include this coverage, but it is good to be aware of its existence, in order not to be caught off-guard.
clues.summary: A low-quality camera with a wide round car blur that makes images look gloomy. You often see the unblurred back of a white car. Good maps usually exclude it.

clues.title: Plants: banana plantations in the south
text: The majority of banana plantations are found in the south.

images.caption: Circle zooms in on banana plants on the terraced hillside

clues.summary: Most banana plantations are in the south.

clues.title: Landscape: flat misty plateau, wind turbines
text: The centre-west of the island is home to an **elevated plateau**. It can be recognized by the unusual flatness, misty coverage, and the presence of wind turbines.
clues.summary: The centre-west has an elevated plateau that is unusually flat, misty, with wind turbines.

clues.title: Guardrail: black-and-yellow below odd mountains
text: The road east of the plateau can be recognized by its unique mountain formations and the black-and-yellow guardrail on the side of the road.
clues.summary: The road east of the plateau has unique mountain shapes and a black-and-yellow guardrail.

clues.title: Landscape: arid, almost no plants
text: The eastern tip of the island is very arid with little to no vegetation.
clues.summary: The eastern tip of the island is very dry with little or no vegetation.

clues.title: Road: dark tarmac, brownish bare soil
text: The ER211 can be recognized by the dark pavement combined with its exposed brownish soil.
clues.summary: Road ER211 has dark pavement and exposed brownish soil.

clues.title: Landscape: high peak, white radar station
text: **Pico Areeiro** is the second highest mountain on the island, and the highest with coverage. It can be recognized by its view over most of the island, and the white radar station at the top.

images.caption: A white radar dome on the high peak, circled in red.

clues.summary: Pico Areeiro, the second highest mountain and highest with coverage, has a view over most of the island and a white radar station at the top.

clues.title: Landscape: lone rock on a raised hill
text: The **Penha d'Águia** is located in northeastern Madeira, isolated on an elevated hill.
clues.summary: Penha d'Águia, in the northeast, stands isolated on a raised hill.

clues.title: Airport: built on many concrete pillars

clues.title: Language: street words, Rua and avenida
text: The word for street in Portuguese is "Rua". Keep in mind that north of Portugal in Spain you can sometimes see streets called "Rúa" (note accent). Here are some other words for "street" in portuguese.
**avenida** - avenue
**calçada** - path/walkway
**autoestrada** - highway
**estrada** - road

images.caption: A tiled street sign reading Rua das Pedras Negras

clues.summary: Rua is street. Other words: avenida (avenue), calçada (path), autoestrada (motorway), estrada (road). Spanish Galicia writes Rúa.

clues.title: Language: ã, -ção, nh, lh endings
text: Most commonly you can look for the letter ã in combination with a few other hints in order to recognize portuguese, especially words ending in -ção. Here are a few other things to look for:
Common two-letter words: ao, as, às, da, de, do, em, os, ou, um
Common three-letter words: aos, com, das, dos, ele, ela, mas, não, por, que, são, uma
Common endings: -ção, -dade, -ismo, -mente
Common digraphs: ch, nh, lh; examples: chave, galinha, baralho.
Of all the major romance languages, Spanish and Portugeuse are the two most similar sharing many words including using the word "PARE" for "STOP" in South America.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Look for ã and words ending in -ção, -dade, -ismo or -mente. Common words: não, são, com, por, que. Digraphs nh and lh. Spanish and Portuguese share many words, including PARE for stop in South America.

clues.title: Language: nh, lh and da/do word contractions
text: Portuguese is a Romance language closely related to Spanish. Spanish and Portuguese can look very similar. Some key differences between the two:
**Ñ** is unique to Spanish.
**Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, Ê** and **lh** are unique to Portuguese (**Ç** is also present in Catalan).
Portuguese uses the **-ao** word ending, and **-nh-** instead of **ñ**.
Spanish uses **de** and **del**, while these are often contracted to **da**, **do**, **das** and **dos** in Portuguese.
The Portuguese word for road is **Rua**.

clues.summary: Portuguese uses -ao endings and nh instead of ñ, plus lh. Spanish de and del are often contracted to da, do, das and dos. Ñ only exists in Spanish; Ç, Ã, Õ, Â, Ê only in Portuguese.

differs.how: Spanish has Ñ and del instead of do/da
